name: San Marcos Tlalcoyalco Popoloca
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Language not in the catalog. The single sweep item (Machin/Stark & Stark 1977, 'Stress and tone in Tlacoyalco Popoloca') is exactly a word-stress description of this language. The Glottolog URL is dead and the live SIL PDF is Cloudflare-blocked, but the SIL Archives entries 8576 (chapter) and 8769 (full volume PIL 54) were located and both PDFs fetched sources from the Wayback Machine (Sept/Aug 2024 captures) into, with lines added. The scans have no text layer; pp. 69-73 were scanned (tesseract, 300 dpi, one at a time) and the stress pages checked against the page images. Deciding statement (pp. 69-71): two length-cued stress types, one per word; consonant stress (the common type) on the ultima in nearly all words and shifting to the ultima under suffixation; vowel stress (20-25% of morphemes) on ultima or penult, moving to the penult under suffixation; suffix-specific type switches. Coding proposal: final (ultima) stress, length-cued, with a lexical consonant/vowel-stress contrast and morphological penult cases. Two further records surfaced during the sweep and are listed as items: the SIL audio companion (entry 57642, not downloaded, no text) and Kalstrom & Pike 1968 on Eastern (Atzingo) Popoloca (other variety, paywalled DOI, not read). The earlier on-disk Rosetta excerpt (pp. 72-83) does not contain the stress section; the new full scan does. No catalog source exists to supersede.

new_statements.quote: Todas las palabras ngiguas llevan acento. El acento en ngigua tiene la función de alargar la vocal de la penúltima sílaba de la palabra o una de las consonantes de la última sílaba, de las siguientes maneras: [3.1] Si una palabra tiene acento vocálico, se acentúa la vocal de la penúltima sílaba y la vocal acentuada tiene una duración prolongada. Si la última sílaba de una palabra empieza con vocal, la vocal de la penúltima sílaba es alargada. [...] [3.2] Cuando el acento alarga una consonante, la consonante alargada siempre pertenece a la última sílaba
new_statements.translation: All Ngigua words carry accent. In Ngigua the accent has the function of lengthening the vowel of the penultimate syllable of the word or one of the consonants of the last syllable, in the following ways: [3.1] If a word has vowel accent, the vowel of the penultimate syllable is accented and the accented vowel has prolonged duration. If the last syllable of a word begins with a vowel, the vowel of the penultimate syllable is lengthened. [...] [3.2] When the accent lengthens a consonant, the lengthened consonant always belongs to the last syllable
new_statements.citation: Stark Campbell, Sharon, con la colaboración de Verónica Luna Villanueva. 2011. Gramática ngigua de San Marcos Tlacoyalco. Cuarta edición, versión electrónica. México, D.F.: Instituto Lingüístico de Verano, A.C. Sección 3 'El acento prosódico', 3.1 'El acento vocálico', 3.2 'El acento consonántico'.

Si la última sílaba de una palabra empi…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Right-edge-bound, duration-based accent of two types: consonant accent lengthens a consonant of the word-final syllable (the saltillo if there is one, else j in a cluster, else the n of an n-cluster, else the single onset consonant), while vowel accent lengthens the vowel of the penultimate syllable. Vowel accent is automatic when the final syllable is vowel-initial (ni.o, nchi.a, na.a); before a consonant-initial final syllable the choice between penult vowel accent (ta.thii.ta, naa.gua, daa.na) and final consonant accent (kathe, kachro, jinda) is lexical and is marked in the orthography by a double vowel. The accent stays at the right edge when suffixes are added (kathe 'huarache' > kathena 'mi huarache', n lengthened; ni'ngo 'iglesia' > ningua 'tu iglesia', u lengthened and saltillo lost). Stark & Machin 1977 analyse the same system as 'consonant stress' vs 'vowel stress' (p. 72, 79-80). Closest fixed-list label: final syllable (consonant type) alternating with penult (vowel type); cf. sister language San Juan Atzingo Popoloca, coded morphological (root-final) in the catalog.
new_statements.exceptions: Footnote 3 (p. 11): words ending in two vowels almost always have vowel accent, but some consonant-accent words end in two vowels; then the two vowels form one syllable and the accent falls on a consonant of that last syllable (chrjuin 'bonito', kjui 'se fue', in.kjaon 'seis', de.jua 'duerme', jai.kua 'rápidamente', jie 'grande'). 3.2.1: the saltillo always takes the accent; when a suffix moves the accent to a new syllable the saltillo is lost (1977 p. 79 gives the same rule: žo²ʔ·o² > žo·¹a²).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('la palabra'), including possessed forms with suffixes; the description is of the citation-form word; tone (three levels) is independent of accent (ch. 2). The 1977 paper treats the domain as the phonological word and notes phrase-level tone lowering only.
new_statements.identity_note: The 2011 grammar describes exactly the variety of San Marcos Tlacoyalco, municipio de Tlacotepec, Puebla (subject language code pls = Glottolog sanm1301), under the autonym Ngigua; the 1977 paper calls the same variety 'Tlacoyalco Popoloca' / 'Northern Popoloca'. Author-order note: Glottolog lists the 1977 chapter as Machin & Stark, but its running head, Adamou 2025 and DiCanio 2012 all give Stark & Machin.

new_statements.quote: Tlacoyalco Popoloca, like Eastern Popoloca (Kalstrom and Pike 1968), has two types of word stress, consonant stress and vowel stress. Every (phonological) word has one or the other, but never both. The predominant contrastive feature of stress is length. [p. 69] ... In nearly all words with consonant stress, the stress occurs on the ultima. When a suffix is added, the stress moves. [p. 70] ... Vowel stress moves to the penult. ... only about twenty to twenty-five per cent of the morphemes in our lexicon have vowel stress. [p. 71]
new_statements.citation: Stark, Sharon & Polly Machin. 1977. Stress and tone in Tlacoyalco Popoloca. In William R. Merrifield (ed.), Studies in Otomanguean phonology (SIL Publications in Linguistics 54), 69-92. Dallas: SIL & UT Arlington.
new_statements.locator: sec. 1 'The Word', pp. 69-71 (PDF pages 7-9); the two deciding sentences are on p. 70 (consonant stress) and p. 71 (vowel stress)
new_statements.reading: One stress per phonological word, cued by length rather than pitch. The majority type (consonant stress, ~75-80% of morphemes) is on the ultima in nearly all words and re-aligns to the ultima after most suffixes; the minority type (vowel stress) is lexically on the ultima or penult and moves to the penult under suffixation; suffix-specific rules switch a word between the two types. For a stress-position catalog this is a predominantly final-stress language (ultima), with a lexical consonant/vowel stress contrast and a morphologically conditioned penultimate pattern; stress placement is largely predictable from word edge plus morphology, the type (consonant vs vowel) being the lexical part.

sources.note: Ch. 3 'El acento prosódico' (printed pp. 11-13, PDF pp. 18-20): every word carries accent; the accent lengthens either the vowel of the penultimate syllable (acento vocálico) or a consonant of the last syllable (acento consonántico); vowel accent is automatic when the final syllable begins with a vowel, otherwise written with a double vowel (ta.thii.ta); consonant accent lengthens the saltillo if present, else j in a cluster, else the n of an n-cluster, else the single onset consonant of the final syllable; accent moves onto a suffix (kathe > kathena, ni'ngo > ningua).

sources.note: First-hand SIL description. Every phonological word carries exactly one stress, of one of two lexically distributed types cued by length: consonant stress (lengthening of the onset consonant of the stressed syllable; in clusters the laryngeal, else /n/, is lengthened) and vowel stress (lengthening of the vowel; on the second vowel of a two-vowel cluster). Consonant stress, the majority type (75-80% of morphemes), falls on the ultima in nearly all words and shifts to the new ultima when a suffix is added (three suffixes -na 'we/our', -ra 'you/your', -ba 'animal' do not trigger the shift).
